sections.h2: Which Montgomery County offices handle a property tax bill?
sections.html:
Two offices in the County Administration Building, 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422, split the work. The Auditor sets values and runs appeals, and the Treasurer bills and collects. The Auditor's line is 937-225-4326, and the Board of Revision application is requested at 937-496-6856.

The Treasurer's page lists 937-225-4010 and weekday hours from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m.. Taxpayer Services is Option 1 on that line, and the delinquency specialists are Option 2. The county's Treasurer FAQ also lists a Semi-Annual Property Charge for solid waste services, with questions going to 937-224-8463.

sections.h2: When are Montgomery County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Taxes are due every February and July, with bills mailed in January and June. The 2026 due dates were February 13 and July 24, both now past. The Treasurer's paying page says a 10% penalty hits any half that is not paid in full by its date.

The county bills one entire year in arrears. The first-half bill covers January through June of the prior calendar year, and the second-half bill covers July through December of that year. Manufactured homes are billed in the actual calendar year instead, and their questions go to (937) 225-5255.

  • No discount exists for paying the whole year in February. Differences between the halves are assessments, some of which appear only on the first-half bill.
  • If a mortgage servicer pays from escrow, tell them you received a bill so they can request a copy.
  • A prepayment plan spreads taxes across monthly bills for owners with no past-due taxes, with enrollment at least 60 days before a half-year due date. Coupons go out at the start of March and August.

sections.h2: What is the 2026 reappraisal and when do new values start?
sections.html:
State law requires a full reappraisal in 2026, and the Auditor adjusts values from each property's grade, condition and style and from recent valid sales. The county's reappraisal FAQ says the new values take effect at the start of 2027 and show up in bills paid in 2027. They do not change the taxes paid during 2026.

Montgomery County 2026 reappraisal steps, per the Auditor's project timeline
WhenStep
July 2026Tentative value notices mailed
July and August 2026Informal review meetings by Zoom or phone
December 2026Final values go to the Department of Taxation for approval
January through March 2027Board of Revision window to appeal final values

The informal review period has ended. The Property Owner Hotline is 937-224-8927 and Spanish assistance is 937-496-3260. A bigger value does not mean an equally bigger bill, since levies decide the tax rate, a point the FAQ makes with a 19% value rise.

sections.h2: How can you contest a Montgomery County property value?
sections.html:
File a complaint with the Auditor's Board of Revision between early January and March 31. The board investigates every complaint and may hold a formal hearing, and the owner must justify the claim. The board can raise or lower a value.

The county's reappraisal FAQ names the evidence that tends to help:

  • A record of an open-market sale of the property in the last three years.
  • An appraisal from the last three years.
  • Sales of comparable properties.
  • Photos or repair estimates that document condition problems.

The same FAQ explains that the Auditor counts only valid sales: open-market deals between a willing buyer and seller. It sets aside sales between relatives, multi-property sales, sheriff's and bank sales, foreclosure auctions and quit-claim transfers. A value can also rise because a levy passed, and a property whose value fell can still see a higher bill if the effective tax rate went up.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for the Montgomery County homestead reduction?
sections.html:
The Treasurer's FAQ says the Homestead Reduction Program is open to owners aged 65 or older and to owners who are totally and permanently disabled. Only an owner-occupied primary residence qualifies. The county's Homestead page carries the application details, so call the Auditor at 937-225-4326 with questions about income limits.

When the house is sold, the value statement filed with the Auditor asks the seller whether a reduction was in effect. Section 319.202 of the Ohio Revised Code requires the buyer to record either that the seller said no reduction applies, or a sworn estimate of the reduction both sides have priced in. A homestead owner who sells should mention the credit to the title company early.

sections.h2: How do you change a mailing address or prove what you paid?
sections.html:
Ohio law requires address changes for a tax bill to be submitted in writing to the Treasurer, and the county posts a Change of Address form for that purpose. A seller who has moved out before closing should file it so the next bill is not lost.

The Treasurer does not mail payment histories on its own. If you pay through mortgage escrow, the amount withheld appears on the 1099 form from the lender. Without records of your own, call 937-225-4010, Option 1, and request an itemization of what was paid. To see how a bill is split among schools, townships and other districts, enter your parcel on the Auditor's site and open the Levy Distribution item, or call 937-225-4326.

sections.h2: What if Montgomery County taxes are late or a lien was sold?
sections.html:
The Treasurer offers delinquent payment plans. An owner who signs a monthly contract pays toward the new taxes while paying off the old ones, without additional interest and penalty. Start at the Treasurer's office or at 937-225-4010, Option 2.

A sold tax lien is different. The county says you cannot make payments on a sold lien through the Treasurer; you arrange payment with the company that bought it. To check release status, look in the Master Information section of the property record on the Treasurer's search page. If the page still reads lien sold, the lien has not been released, even if the holder was paid. A buyer's title company will look for that line, so clear it before you list.

sections.h2: What does Montgomery County look like for owners and sellers?
sections.html:
Dayton anchors the county, which the 2020 census counted at 537,309 people, the fifth most in Ohio, in about 464 square miles, per Wikipedia. The county's FAQ puts the parcel count near 230,000.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts shows 231,319 households averaging 2.24 people. Selected monthly costs for owners are a median of $1,438 with a mortgage and $604 without one, and about 86% of residents stayed in the same house across a year. The county issued 1,079 building permits in 2025.

Those figures give context when you read an escrow statement or compare an offer to the tax bill. Ask the Treasurer for the payoff on your parcel before closing, and ask your title company how it splits a bill that covers a prior year.

faqs.q: When is the second-half Montgomery County property tax payment due?
faqs.a: It falls in July each year, and the 2026 date was July 24. The first-half payment is due in February, and in 2026 that date was February 13.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for paying Montgomery County property taxes late?
faqs.a: The Treasurer applies a 10% penalty to any first-half or second-half payment not paid in full by its due date.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my Montgomery County property value?
faqs.a: File with the Board of Revision from the start of January through March 31. For the 2026 reappraisal, the county says the window for the new values opens January 1, 2027.

faqs.q: Do I get a discount for paying a whole year of Montgomery County taxes in February?
faqs.a: No. The Treasurer says there is no discount for paying the full year at once, and the difference between the two halves comes from assessments.

faqs.q: Can I pay a sold tax lien at the Montgomery County Treasurer?
faqs.a: No. Once a lien is sold, you arrange payments with the lien holder, and you confirm the release by checking that the record no longer says lien sold.
